examiner_notes.quote: It has been mentioned in previous examiners reports that the use of a diagram would aid candidates understanding of a question and this was such a case.
For many candidates this was a straightforward question and there were lots of fully correct responses.
Unfortunately subtracting vectors when they should have been added, and vice versa, had huge consequences.
In part (a) candidates simply had to use OA AB + to find OB .
examiner_notes.display: In part (a) candidates simply had to use $\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AB}$ to find $\overrightarrow{OB}$ .

examiner_notes.quote: The answer could be given in coordinate or vector form and many achieved one of the correct versions.
There were the usual slips when adding but both marks were lost when candidates attempted a subtraction.
In part (b) candidates were required to use the fact thatOC was perpendicular to BC .
examiner_notes.display: In part (b) candidates were required to use the fact that $\overrightarrow{OC}$ was perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{BC}$ .

examiner_notes.display: Successful candidates used the fact that $\overrightarrow{OC}.\overrightarrow{BC}=0$ to set up an equation in a which could be easily solved.

examiner_notes.quote: Errors and a general misunderstanding of the geometry in this part of the question were common, many of which could have been addressed by a well labelled diagram.
Reasons for a loss of marks here were:
• a failure to find vector BC via OC OB − • a failure to understand which vectors were perpendicular or else setting . OC BC equal to something other than 0 such as 1
examiner_notes.display: • a failure to find vector $\overrightarrow{BC}$ via $\overrightarrow{OC}-\overrightarrow{OB}$ • a failure to understand which vectors were perpendicular or else setting . $\overrightarrow{OC}.\overrightarrow{BC}$ equal to something other than 0 such as 1

examiner_notes.quote: This was the second question on vectors and another in which it would have been beneficial to draw a diagram. Parts (a) and (b) were relatively straightforward with part (c) being very discriminating even at grade A standard.
In part (a) candidates were required to use the fact that 5 10 OA = where A was a point on the given line to show that 2 81 220 0 52 − + =   .
examiner_notes.display: In part (a) candidates were required to use the fact that $|\overrightarrow{OA}|=5\sqrt{10}$ where A was a point on the given line to show that $81\lambda^2+52\lambda-220=0$ .

examiner_notes.quote: Most knew what to do, although a huge error was committed by some who used just the gradient vector as opposed to the point ( ) , , 1 8 2 5 4 + − +    when finding OA .
examiner_notes.display: Most knew what to do, although a huge error was committed by some who used just the gradient vector as opposed to the point $(1+8\lambda,2-\lambda,5+4\lambda)$ when finding $|\overrightarrow{OA}|$ .

examiner_notes.quote: Errors were rare but seen when candidates failed to correctly square 5 10 or else not showing sufficient steps in the proof.
examiner_notes.display: Errors were rare but seen when candidates failed to correctly square $5\sqrt{10}$ or else not showing sufficient steps in the proof.

examiner_notes.quote: Part (b) involved solving the given equation and using the values of  to find the two positions of A. The point ( ) 15, 4, 3 − − was given and it was important to show all steps leading to this answer.
A score of 1, 0, 1 was common when candidates assumed they could just write down a given answer.
Part (c) could be attempted by various methods including via the scalar product or the cosine rule.
Good candidates drew a diagram and could easily determine what was required.
Once the angle was found via scalar product or the cosine rule, the area of the triangle could be found via the formula 1 sin 2 OA OB AOB  .
examiner_notes.display: Once the angle was found via scalar product or the cosine rule, the area of the triangle could be found via the formula $\dfrac{1}{2}OA\times OB\sin AOB$ .

examiner_notes.quote: A very common error in part (c) worthy of note was in determining the angle AOB. The most straightforward way was via the scalar product of 15 4 3   −       −   and 8 1 4     −       , but many if not most candidates, tried to find vector OB using its length which, although a valid method, did introduce aspects that could lead to slips in calculations.
examiner_notes.display: A very common error in part (c) worthy of note was in determining the angle AOB. The most straightforward way was via the scalar product of $\begin{pmatrix}-15\\4\\-3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}8\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}$, but many if not most candidates, tried to find vector OB using its length which, although a valid method, did introduce aspects that could lead to slips in calculations.
